[...] su morfología es aglutinante pues los morfemas son segmentables, a excepción de la marcación del perfecto que se marca a través de sustracción de la vocal final (Reyes Taboada, 2021). new_statements.translation: Unlike other Nahua languages, in Mexicanero stress is not always located on the penultimate syllable, but has grammatical functions (Canger 2000; Castro Medina 2000). [...] its morphology is agglutinative since the morphemes are segmentable, except for perfect marking, which is marked by subtraction of the final vowel. [...] As for stress, in this work it is marked on all forms that do not have it on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate stress is the default (unmarked in the orthography); but because Mexicanero has lost historical final vowels/syllables (plural -m < -meh, plural-subject -l < -lo, noun endings -l < -li, perfective formed by dropping the final vowel), many surface forms carry final stress and stress thereby contrasts and signals grammatical categories (e.g. Canger 2001 for the sister variety: kitása 'he throws it' vs kitasá 'he threw it'; text forms takám 'men', kochíl 'they sleep', yowál 'night', tamál).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in grammatically/lexically determined forms (apocopated plurals, plural-subject verbs, perfectives, nouns like yowál, tamál, Spanish-type loans like xuravét); Canger 2000 (sister variety) adds that the antepenult is occasionally stressed and that consonant-final adverbs are final-stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation and text forms; author is an INAH fieldworker on the San Pedro de Xícoras variety and applies the convention to her own transcribed text; the analytic claim is backed by citation of Canger 2000 (San Agustín de Buenaventura) and Castro Medina 2000 (San Pedro Jícora).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Reyes Taboada & Villa Reyes 2023) explicitly describes the San Pedro de Xícoras (= San Pedro Jícora) variety, i.e. Eastern Durango Nahuatl east2695/azd, the same variety Preuss documented. The fuller stress literature it relies on (Canger 2000, 2001) describes San Agustín de Buenaventura, which ISO 2011-111 and Glottolog assign to Western Durango Nahuatl (west2778/azn); Castro Medina 2000 is the San Pedro Jícora description. our earlier survey note that Canger 2001 is 'San Pedro Jicoras' is wrong: Canger 2001 is San Agustín de Buenaventura.
